lead: A title tells you what someone is good at, but it doesn't make everything they say automatically right.
when: When a celebrity endorses something, a speaker has an impressive title, or a team stops discussing because "the boss said so," this model helps.
body:
A teacher, a doctor, or a famous entrepreneur has usually built up a lot of experience in their own field and deserves to be taken seriously. But sometimes we stretch that trust to every topic: because someone succeeded in business, we assume they're also reliable on education, history, and nutrition. That's what authority bias commonly looks like.

Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy or give more weight to an opinion because it comes from an authority figure, without adequately examining the content itself.

The safer approach isn't to reject experts, but to put your trust in the right place. First see whether the person is talking about their own field. Then look at what evidence they offer, whether they explain where things are uncertain, and what other people who know the subject think.
example:
During a livestream, a writer you really admire recommends a paid learning tool. Their books have genuinely helped you, so you want to buy it almost without looking at the features or the price. But being a great writer doesn't mean they know your study habits, or that they've tried every similar product.

You can treat the recommendation as a lead: try the free version first, and check whether you can export your data and whether it actually solves your problem. That way you're not dismissing the writer's experience, but you're also not treating their reputation as reason enough to spend your money.
extra: A teacher who's great at teaching math doesn't necessarily know which career suits each student best. A coworker who ran one successful project doesn't prove that the same plan fits every client. Respecting experience while asking about the conditions isn't rude.
steps: First ask: how closely is what they're saying related to their professional experience?
Then look at the specific evidence, the conditions under which it applies, and whether there's anything you should know about, such as a paid partnership.
For important decisions, find at least one independent source instead of just hearing the same celebrity's view repeated.
caution: "Experts can be wrong too" doesn't mean any random guess is as credible as professional research. What you should compare is relevant experience and evidence, rather than swinging between blind obedience and opposing every expert on principle.
exercise: Take one piece of advice you recently followed and complete two sentences: "What this person is actually good at is..." and "What I still need to check for myself this time is..."
brief: Separating the look of authority from the evidence: on the left, a stick figure at a podium wearing a medal uses a big megaphone to present a geometric idea, and the listeners follow automatically. On the right, an ordinary stick figure examines evidence pieces of the same pattern with a magnifying glass. A broken line between the medal and the truth shows that identity alone can't settle the question.
